head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Quotient and remainder in one call
Peels off one base-x digit `cur` per loop (least significant first)
Position of the digit: it stands for `cur × x^k`
Cost of writing x^k is k operators (k−1 `*` and one `+`); x^0 is `x/x` costing 2
Fewest operators to build the digits processed so far exactly (no overshoot)
State A of the digit DP
Fewest operators to build them as 'next power minus remainder' (overshoot by one unit at this position)
State B: a carry to the next digit
New `pos`: use `cur` copies of x^k on top of exact lower digits, or `cur+1` copies and absorb the overshoot
Final: finish exactly, or take one more x^k and subtract the overshoot; remove one `+` for the first term
The first term needs no leading operator

p: `x = 3`, `target = 19` has base-3 digits 2, 0, 1 (19 = 2·9 + 0·3 + 1), read least significant first by the loop. Result 5 (`3*3+3*3+3/3`):

Any expression is a signed sum of powers of x. A digit of the base-x representation can be built by adding that power cur times, or by overshooting with cur+1 copies and subtracting the missing part at the lower digits (the 'neg' route). Each position needs only two states, so the DP is O(log target). The code agrees with an independent shortest-path search over signed sums of powers for every x from 2 to 5 and target from 1 to 59: True.

964.takeaway: Digit DP in base x: for each digit track the cost with and without a borrow, where x^k costs k operators and x^0 costs 2.

`heapq` is a min-heap; negating makes the FARTHEST point sit at the root
Tuple stores the point with its key
Tuples compare by the first element first
Drop the farthest once there are more than k
The heap always keeps the k closest seen so far
`[[x, y] for _, x, y in heap]`

p: points `[[1,3],[-2,2],[3,3],[0,1]]`, `k = 2` (heap shown as (squared distance, x, y)):

blocks.h: Why a max-heap of size k and not sorting everything?
p: When k is much smaller than n, a heap that holds only the k best candidates is cheaper than sorting. The root is always the worst of the current best k, so it is the one to evict.

973.takeaway: Top-k smallest with a max-heap of size k: push each point, evict the farthest when the heap exceeds k.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Coins the subtree rooted here has left over (negative = needs coins)
This node's own coins minus the one it must keep
Every coin of the excess crosses the edge to the parent (or the parent sends −e coins down)
Each unit of flow on an edge costs one move
Parent adds it to its own balance

p: `[3,0,0]`: total moves = 2 (the root sends one coin to each child). Subtrees finish in this order:
The left child holds 3 coins and keeps 1; its 2 spare coins cross the edge to the root, one of which the root passes to the right child, so flow on the left edge is 2 and on the right edge is 1.

blocks.h: Why does the sum of |excess| equal the minimum moves?
p: Each edge must carry the net imbalance of the subtree below it: if the subtree has e extra coins, at least |e| coins must cross that edge, and moving them straight there is enough. Flows on different edges are independent, so the total is the sum over all edges.

979.takeaway: Count the net coin flow across every edge: for each subtree, |coins − nodes| moves must cross the edge above it.

Lets us stop early and detect unreachable oranges
Process exactly one minute's worth of oranges
`len(q)` is evaluated once, so newly rotten ones wait for the next minute
If any fresh orange remains it was unreachable

p: Rot spreads one step per minute to all neighbours simultaneously. A BFS from all rotten oranges at once explores exactly one distance layer per minute, so the number of layers needed to reach the last fresh orange is the answer. Running BFS separately from each orange would be slower and would not give simultaneous spreading.

994.takeaway: Multi-source BFS (Breadth-First Search) with a level loop: one level = one minute; leftover fresh oranges mean −1.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: The bracket is not the outermost opener
Level 0 → 1 is the primitive piece's first bracket
After closing, still inside a piece
Closing back to level 0 is the outermost closer

blocks.h: Why check depth before incrementing and after decrementing?
p: Both checks ask 'is this bracket at the outermost level?' An opening bracket is outermost if it starts at depth 0; a closing bracket is outermost if it returns to depth 0. Dropping exactly those removes the outer pair of every primitive piece, and primitive pieces are exactly the stretches between consecutive returns to depth 0.

1021.takeaway: Depth counter: skip the bracket that moves depth 0 → 1 and the one that moves 1 → 0.

Minimum is 0, 1 or 2 by the case analysis. As a check, the closed formula equals an exhaustive game search for every starting triple with positions in 1 to 11: True.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Minimum score to triangulate the polygon formed by corners i, i+1, …, j
Interval DP (Dynamic Programming); the edge i–j is the 'base'
Intervals with at least 3 corners, shortest first
`dp[i][k]` and `dp[k][j]` are shorter, so they are ready
The third corner of the triangle that sits on edge i–j
Every triangulation has exactly one such triangle
Plus the two sub-polygons on each side
Edge 0–(n−1) is a polygon side, so it needs a triangle on it

blocks.h: Why pick the triangle on the base edge?
p: In any triangulation of the polygon i..j, the edge (i, j) belongs to exactly one triangle with a third corner k. That triangle splits the rest into polygons i..k and k..j, which are independent subproblems. Trying every k covers all triangulations without repeating any.

1039.takeaway: Interval DP: choose the third corner k of the triangle on edge (i, j); the two sides are independent sub-polygons.

Longest chain ending at word w
Generate every possible predecessor instead of testing every shorter word
Is that predecessor one of the words?

p: `['a','b','ba','bca','bda','bdca']` → 4 (a → ba → bda → bdca):

blocks.h: Why delete letters instead of inserting?
p: Inserting one of 26 letters at each of L+1 positions makes up to 26·(L+1) candidates. Deleting one of L letters makes only L candidates, and each is looked up in the dict. Sorting by length guarantees shorter words already have their dp values.

bullets: Time: O(n·L²): n words, L deletions each, each building and hashing an L-character string (plus O(n log n) for sorting).

1048.takeaway: DP over words sorted by length: for each word try deleting each letter and extend the chain of that predecessor.

What it does
When to reach for it

Pairs the actual and expected height at each position

blocks.h: Why does comparing with the sorted list count the right students?
p: The sorted array is the only non-decreasing arrangement, so the expected height at each position is fixed. Every position whose actual height differs from it is a student out of place. Ties between equal heights don't create mismatches because equal values are interchangeable.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort.
Space: O(n) for the sorted copy (a counting sort can make it O(n + range)).

1051.takeaway: Sort a copy and count the positions where the original differs.

What it does
When to reach for it

All worker–bike pairs sorted by distance, then worker index, then bike index
Tuple order encodes the problem's tie-break rules exactly
Worker still free and bike still free
Skip pairs that are no longer available

p: workers `[[0,0],[2,1]]`, bikes `[[1,2],[3,3]]` → `[1, 0]`. Pairs in sorted order (distance, worker, bike):

blocks.h: Why does the sorted scan equal the repeated 'pick the smallest' rule?
p: The rule says: among all unassigned pairs pick the smallest (distance, worker, bike). A sorted list visits pairs in exactly that order, and skipping already-used workers or bikes is the same as 'among unassigned pairs'. So one pass reproduces the repeated selection.

bullets: Time: O(W·B log(W·B)) for sorting all pairs.
Space: O(W·B) for the pair list.

1057.takeaway: Greedy by sorted (distance, worker, bike) tuples; skip pairs whose worker or bike is already used.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: How many numbers are missing before index mid
With no gaps, `nums[mid] = nums[0] + mid`; the excess is the count of missing numbers
Fewer than k missing numbers up to mid
The k-th missing number lies to the right
Finds the first index where missing ≥ k (possibly `len(nums)`)
The answer from the first index with ≥ k missing
Count k missing numbers starting from the last array element before `lo`

p: Result 8 (missing numbers are 5, 6, 8, 11, …).

After the search `lo` is the first index where the missing count is at least k, so the k-th missing number is beyond `nums[lo-1]`. There are `missing(lo-1) = nums[lo-1] - nums[0] - (lo-1)` missing before it, and the answer is `nums[lo-1] + (k - missing(lo-1))`, which simplifies to `nums[0] + lo - 1 + k`. For `k = 3` the search ends at `lo = 2`: `nums[1] = 7` has 2 missing numbers before it (5 and 6), so the 3rd missing number is 7 + (3 − 2) = 8.

1060.takeaway: Binary search on 'missing count before index mid', then compute the answer arithmetically from the boundary.

rows: Position of the next closing brace
Find the end of the option group
So the product comes out in alphabetical order
A plain letter as a one-option group
Treat letters and brace groups uniformly
Cartesian product of the groups, from `itertools`
All combinations of one choice per group; the last group varies fastest
Join one combination into a word

p: `{a,b}c{d,e}f` is parsed into groups `[['a', 'b'], ['c'], ['d', 'e'], ['f']]`, and the product gives `['acdf', 'acef', 'bcdf', 'bcef']`:

blocks.h: Why sorting groups is enough for sorted output
p: `itertools.product` yields tuples in lexicographic order with respect to the input groups. If every group is sorted, the joined words are in alphabetical order whenever all options are single letters (as here). No final sort is needed.

bullets: Time: O(number of results × length) to generate; parsing is O(n).
Space: O(number of results × length) for the output.

1087.takeaway: Parse the pattern into option groups, then take the Cartesian product (itertools.product) of the sorted groups.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Counter allowing at most 2 hydrogen threads past `acquire()` at once
Limits each molecule to two H
Limits each molecule to one O
`wait()` blocks until 3 threads have called it, then releases all three together
Gathers exactly 2 H + 1 O before any of them outputs
Lets the next molecule's atoms proceed
The callbacks that print the letter
Called only after the barrier opens

p: Running 8 hydrogen and 4 oxygen threads started in random order produced these outputs (each 3-letter group is one molecule; 'valid' means every group has exactly 2 H and 1 O):

blocks.h: Why is a barrier not enough alone, and why are semaphores not enough alone?
bullets: Barrier alone: three hydrogens could meet at the barrier and leave together, producing HHH.
Semaphores alone: they cap how many H/O are admitted but do not make them print together, so letters of different molecules could interleave.

Together: the semaphores admit at most 2 H and 1 O, so the 3 threads waiting at the barrier are always 2 H + 1 O; the barrier then releases them as one molecule, and the permits are returned only after printing so the next molecule cannot start early.
Time: O(n) thread operations for n molecules (each atom acquires, waits once and releases).

1117.takeaway: Combine counting semaphores (limit 2 H and 1 O) with a barrier of 3 so exactly one molecule forms at a time.

p: Tree `[3,5,1,6,2,0,8,null,null,7,4]` → node 2. Nodes in post-order, with the answer node each returns:

blocks.h: Why does equal depth make the node the LCA?
p: If both children's subtrees reach the same maximum depth, the deepest leaves of this subtree lie on both sides, so the lowest node containing all of them is the current node. If one side is deeper, all deepest leaves are on that side and the answer was already found inside it.

1123.takeaway: Return (depth, LCA) from each subtree: equal child depths make the current node the LCA of the deepest leaves.

`ord('a') = 97`; letters are laid out in rows of five
Build a run of identical moves
Move left and up first, down and right last
Keeps the path on the board (see below)

p: `'leet'` → `DDR!UURRR!!DDD!`:

blocks.h: Why left and up before down and right?
p: The only awkward cell is `z`, alone in row 5 (column 0). To go TO z you must be in column 0 first and then move down, so the left move must come before the down move. To go FROM z you must move up before moving right, since row 5 has no cells to the right of z. The order L, U, D, R satisfies both. Checking every path of the form a→b→a for all letter pairs by simulation, none leaves the board: True.

bullets: Time: O(n) for a target of n letters (each move string is at most 9 characters).

1138.takeaway: Convert letters to (row, col) with divmod and always emit L and U before D and R so the lone z row is entered and left safely.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: All land cells as BFS (Breadth-First Search) sources
Distance to the nearest land = BFS layer from all lands at once
Answer is −1; `in` with a tuple tests both
`dist` starts at −1 so the land layer itself is layer 0 and the final empty-layer pass doesn't overcount
Mark water as visited by turning it into land

p: `[[1,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,1]]` → 2. In pass d the queue holds cells at distance d from land; the water cells they reach are at distance d+1:

blocks.h: Why does the final value of `dist` equal the answer?
p: `dist` starts at −1 and increases at the start of each pass. Pass 0 expands the land cells themselves, pass 1 the cells at distance 1, and so on. The last pass (here pass 2) expands the farthest water cells and finds nothing new, so `dist` equals the distance of the farthest water cell from land: the cell (1,1) is 2 steps away.

1162.takeaway: Multi-source BFS (Breadth-First Search) from every land cell: the number of layers needed to cover all water is the answer.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Edge from a virtual node 0 to house i+1 with cost = well cost
Building a well becomes 'connect this house to the water source'
Sort all edges by cost (first tuple element)
Kruskal's minimum spanning tree: consider the cheapest edges first
Each node starts as its own group
Root of x's group, flattening the tree on the way
The edge joins two separate groups
Skip edges that would form a cycle

p: n = 3, wells `[1,2,2]`, pipes `[[1,2,1],[2,3,1]]` → 3 (well at house 1, then pipes 1–2 and 2–3):

Without it, houses can get water from a well or a pipe, two different kinds of choices. Adding node 0 as a 'water source' and treating each well as a pipe from node 0 to its house makes every house need to be connected to node 0 in a graph, which is exactly a minimum spanning tree over n+1 nodes. A well is then just an edge to node 0.

bullets: Time: O(E log E) for sorting, with E = n + number of pipes.

1168.takeaway: Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal with Union-Find) after modelling each well as an edge to a virtual source node 0.

What it does
When to reach for it
rows: The whole prefix may be deleted, so a node with prefix sum 0 must exist
For each prefix sum, remember the LAST node that has it
A later node with the same prefix sum means everything in between sums to 0
Skip from the current node straight to just after the last node with the same prefix
Cuts the zero-sum stretch out in one pointer change
Two nodes with equal prefix sums enclose a zero-sum run

p: `1→2→−3→3→1` → 3→1. First pass (prefix sum after each node, starting at the dummy):
At the dummy (prefix 0), `last[0]` is the node with value −3 (prefix 0 again), so the dummy jumps over 1, 2, −3. The resulting list is `3→1`.

head: Node value
Prefix sum
Action
rows: next jumps to node after last[0] (3)
next jumps to node after last[3] (1)
next jumps to node after last[4] (None)

blocks.h: Why the LAST node with each prefix sum?
p: If the same prefix sum occurs at nodes p < q, the nodes strictly between them sum to 0. Jumping to the last such node removes the longest zero-sum stretch at once, including any zero-sum sublists inside it, so no repeated deletions are needed.

1171.takeaway: Prefix sums with last-occurrence jumping: equal prefix sums enclose a zero-sum run, so link to the node after the last equal one.
